rows.verified: Warehouse risk assessments should cover the main causes of injury and ill health, including manual handling and moving vehicles.
Risk assessments should consider times when vehicle or pedestrian movements change, such as shift changes.
Where appropriate, lorry movements can be stopped during shift changes to reduce vehicle-pedestrian interaction.
Warehouse safety management should address mechanical handling, site transport, work at height and manual handling.
Storage and warehousing controls should apply across facilities of different sizes, including specialist temperature-controlled or dangerous-substance stores.
Warehouse procedures should cover avoidable hazards, accident prevention and emergency arrangements.
Warehouse controls need to account for employees and other people working around the facility, including hauliers and couriers.
Responsible storage practices require coordinated controls for movement, stacking, access, equipment and worker information.
Warehouse controls depend on goods, racking, stacking height, lift trucks, loading bays, pedestrian flows, shift patterns, temperature, fire load and emergency arrangements.
Warehousing evidence is facility-, inventory-, operation- and time-specific and is not an exact parcel-level injury or fire probability.
PUWER requires work equipment to be maintained in an efficient state, efficient working order and good repair.
Where machinery has a maintenance log, the log must be kept up to date and maintenance operations must be capable of being carried out safely.
Maintenance should be planned using manufacturer information and a safe system of work, with competent people and suitable tools.
Maintenance areas need safe access, and barriers or signs may be required to protect other workers and contractors.
Before maintenance, moving machinery should be stopped and electrical, hydraulic, pneumatic and other energy sources isolated and locked off where necessary.
Stored energy should be released safely, unsupported parts secured, pressurised systems isolated and hot components allowed to cool.
Inspection frequency should be based on risk, installation conditions, deterioration and exceptional events that could affect safety.
Inspection results should be recorded and retained at least until the next inspection, and equipment should not be used without evidence that required inspection occurred.
Maintenance controls depend on equipment, energy sources, failure mode, access, isolation points, stored energy, contractor interfaces, production state and worker competence.
Maintenance evidence is equipment-, task-, energy- and site-specific and is not an exact parcel-level injury probability.
